title: Vibe Coding Basics
description: Your first steps in vibe coding: turn a real campus problem into a real app with GitHub Copilot.
keywords: Basics

title: What is vibe coding?
description: Lesson 1
keywords: Vibe coding means building an application by describing what you want to an AI, instead of writing every line of code yourself. With GitHub Copilot, you explain your need in plain language and the AI proposes the code; you stay in charge — you read, adjust, and approve. For higher education, this changes everything: you can finally build the small tool you've imagined for years, without waiting on an IT department or spending six months learning to program. This track walks you through it step by step, using one real teaching project as your thread. Whatever your role — teaching, studying, IT, HR, management, finance — write down, in one sentence, the small app you'd love to have. You'll build a real one in Lesson 3.

title: From a real campus problem to an app idea
description: Lesson 2
keywords: The best starting point is never a technology, it is a real campus problem: students have no easy way to revise, a service keeps answering the same question by email, a team tracks a budget line in ten spreadsheets, a lab needs a lightweight booking page. Start from lived friction. Describe the problem in one sentence, then imagine the smallest possible app that would reduce that friction. A quiz, a page, a calculator, a tracker, a searchable FAQ: keep it simple first, then grow it once people are actually using it. Pick ONE real problem you or a colleague complains about weekly — in class, at the help desk, during onboarding, in a budget meeting — and write your app idea using the sentence above.

title: Your first web app with GitHub Copilot
description: Lesson 3
keywords: This is the lesson where you actually build something. Install the GitHub Copilot extension in Visual Studio Code, or open Copilot Chat directly on github.com/copilot with your GitHub account, then create a new file called index.html. Below, we build a real, working example together — a “Quick Poll” you could use in a class, a training session, a team meeting, or a town hall. Follow the steps with your own copy of Copilot, then try the finished result live at the end. Rebuild this exact Quick Poll yourself in a new index.html file, then change the question and the four options to match your own role — a class topic, an onboarding question, a budget priority, anything real to you.

title: Saving and publishing with GitHub
description: Lesson 4
keywords: Once your first version works, create a repository on GitHub and push your code to it — this is called a commit. From that point on, your work is saved online, versioned, and you can always go back to an earlier version if something breaks. Then turn on GitHub Pages for that repository: in a few clicks, your app becomes reachable through a simple link you can share with students or colleagues, with no server to manage. Create a free GitHub account if you don't have one, push your Quick Poll to a brand-new repository, and turn on GitHub Pages for it.

title: Testing and improving with Copilot Chat
description: Lesson 5
keywords: Have one or two colleagues try your app, or test it yourself by putting yourself in a student's shoes. Note every bug or awkward moment, then describe them one by one to Copilot Chat: “when I click this button, nothing happens, fix it”. Copilot can also explain existing code you don't fully understand yet: ask “explain this part to me” before asking for a change. Send your published link to two colleagues (or classmates) and ask them to click through it. Write down every awkward moment they hit, then fix the first one with Copilot Chat.

title: Improving style and appearance
description: Lesson 6
keywords: Once your app works, ask Copilot to improve the presentation: your institution’s colours, clearer spacing, more readable text, stronger accessibility. You can also create a small Copilot Space with example copy, slides, or a style guide so the suggestions stay grounded in your own material. Think about accessibility too: enough contrast, readable text, clear labels, and buttons that are easy to hit. Ask Copilot to check those points explicitly before you publish. Ask Copilot to restyle your Quick Poll using two colors that represent your institution or team, then open it on your phone to check it still looks good.

title: Adding images, files, and documents
description: Lesson 7
keywords: Many teaching tools need images, PDFs, or downloadable documents: a handout, a diagram, a form. Ask Copilot to add an image display area or a download button, then simply drop the file into your GitHub repository. GitHub hosts your code and these files alike: no need for another tool to store your app's resources. Add one image or one downloadable PDF to your Quick Poll (even a placeholder), commit it, and confirm it loads correctly on the published page.

title: Wrap-up and on to the Advanced track
description: Lesson 8
keywords: You now know how to turn a teaching idea into a real app: build with Copilot, save and publish with GitHub, test, improve the style, add files. The one habit that matters most: always move forward in small, checkable steps. The Advanced track picks up from here to go further: connecting a real database, giving your project a lasting memory, and managing your code with GitHub like a real project meant to last. Write a 3-line README for your project: what it does, who it's for, and how to reopen it with Copilot next time.

title: Vibe Coding Advanced
description: Connect a database, give your project durable instructions, and manage your code like a project that is meant to last.
keywords: Advanced

title: Working with Copilot's agent mode
description: Lesson 1
keywords: Beyond line-by-line suggestions, Copilot offers an agent mode: describe a bigger task (“add a sign-up form to my quiz and make sure it works”), and Copilot plans several changes, applies them, and checks the result, with checkpoints for you to approve. This is the right tool once your app grows and you no longer want to describe every small line one by one. Describe one multi-step task to Copilot's agent mode (for example, adding a results page to your Quick Poll) and review its plan carefully before letting it run.

title: Connecting a database to your app
description: Lesson 2
keywords: As soon as your tool needs to remember information from one session to the next (quiz answers, sign-ups, grades), you need a database. Services like Supabase let you create one for free, with no server setup, and Copilot helps you write the connection code. Describe to Copilot what you want to store (for example: the student's name and their score), and let it propose the database structure and the code needed to read and write to it. Create a free Supabase project and connect it to a small test page that stores just one piece of information, like a name and a vote.

title: Using that database safely
description: Lesson 3
keywords: A poorly protected database can expose your students' data. Always ask Copilot to add security rules (who is allowed to read or write what), and never store more personal information than necessary. Think about your students' data protection from the start (GDPR in Europe): anonymise what can be anonymised, and be clear about what the data you collect is used for. Ask Copilot to review your database code for security issues, and fix at least one thing it flags.

title: Designing consciously for learning
description: Lesson 4
keywords: A good teaching tool isn't just functional, it's designed for learning: immediate feedback after an answer, visible progress, encouragement rather than punishment. Describe these pedagogical intentions to Copilot, not just technical features. For example, instead of “show the score”, ask for “show the score with an explanation for each mistake, so the student understands why they got it wrong”. Rewrite one feature request for your project as a learning-or-user-focused prompt, following the example above, instead of a purely technical one.

title: Writing a solid build plan
description: Lesson 5
keywords: Before asking Copilot for a big feature, write yourself a short plan in a few lines: the steps, the logical order, what's essential and what can wait. A good plan produces far better suggestions than a vague request. Then share this plan with Copilot Chat before you start coding — it can flag missing steps or a more logical order. Write a five-line build plan for your next feature before asking Copilot for any code, then share it with Copilot Chat first.

title: Iterating smartly without breaking your app
description: Lesson 6
keywords: The bigger your project grows, the more tempting it is to ask for several changes at once. Resist that: one change, one test, one commit on GitHub. If something breaks, you know exactly what to undo. GitHub lets you roll back very easily thanks to its commit history: it's your safety net to keep iterating without stress. Make three small, separate commits today, each with one clear change and one clear commit message.

title: Giving your project a lasting memory
description: Lesson 7
keywords: Without specific instructions, Copilot will not automatically keep every project convention in mind. Put a .github/copilot-instructions.md file in the repository and write the rules you repeat every session: naming, tone, build steps, accessibility constraints, or visual conventions. You can complement that with prompt files, path-specific instruction files, AGENTS.md, or specialised agent files later. Start with the single always-on instruction file first so the project stops resetting to “generic mode”. Create your first .github/copilot-instructions.md file with at least three rules that matter in your own context: style, build steps, and one institutional constraint.

title: Using AI as a tester
description: Lesson 8
keywords: Before showing your app to real students, ask Copilot Chat to play a clumsy or distracted user: “try to break this form”, “what happens if I leave this field empty?”. Also ask it to generate test cases: examples of correct, incorrect, or completely unexpected answers to your quiz or form. Ask Copilot Chat to try to break your app in three different ways, then fix whatever it finds.

title: Managing your code like a real project with GitHub
description: Lesson 9
keywords: A project that lasts needs real organisation: clear commits, small branches, pull requests, and a review habit. If your institution wants the GitHub platform at scale, the GitHub Campus Program can provide GitHub Enterprise Cloud or Server to the whole school — but that is the platform layer, not a blanket free Copilot licence for every staff role. For Copilot itself, students can still use Copilot Student individually and verified teachers can still use free Copilot Pro individually. Wider staff rollout across IT, HR, finance, leadership, and administration means planning for Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise with the right governance and budget model. Create a branch, make one small change on it, and open your first pull request to merge it back into your main version.

title: Vibe Coding Expert
description: Add artificial intelligence to your app and build a complete example, ready for a real course.
keywords: Expert

title: Adding AI to your teaching app
description: Lesson 1
keywords: So far, Copilot has helped you write the code of your app. This lesson goes further: adding an AI feature your students can use directly, like an “explain this differently” button that queries an AI model live. Ask Copilot to help you build this integration: a button that sends a question to an AI model and displays the answer on your page. Add one AI-powered button to an existing project — even a placeholder that just echoes the question back — to see the wiring end to end.

title: Choosing and comparing AI models
description: Lesson 2
keywords: Several families of AI models exist (GPT, Claude, Gemini, among others), with differences in quality, speed, and cost. Inside Copilot Chat, you can already pick between several models depending on the task. For the AI built into your teaching app, start simple with an inexpensive model, and only move to a more powerful one if you really need to. Ask the same question to two different models inside Copilot Chat and compare the answers for quality, tone, and speed.

title: Setting up your access keys securely
description: Lesson 3
keywords: To use an AI model in your app, you need an access key (API key): a kind of password for that service. Never put this key directly in code that is visible on GitHub. Ask Copilot to help you store it as a protected secret (environment variable or GitHub secret): your institution's IT department can help with this if needed. Store one API key as a protected secret instead of directly in your code, and confirm your code still works by reading it from there.

title: First small project: an AI explanation button
description: Lesson 4
keywords: Build a concrete example: on your course page, an “I don't understand” button that sends the student's question to an AI model and shows a different explanation, simpler or with another example. Ask Copilot to build this feature step by step, testing each part before moving to the next. Build the “I don't understand” button end to end on a real page you own — your Quick Poll or another project.

title: Deploying your AI integration safely
description: Lesson 5
keywords: An AI integration should never expose your access key in the student's browser. Ask Copilot to set up a small server-side function that receives the question, calls the AI model with the hidden key, and returns only the answer. Platforms like Vercel or Netlify let you host this kind of function for free for a small project, in a few clicks straight from your GitHub repository. Deploy your AI feature through a small serverless function, and check your browser's network tab to confirm the key never appears there.

title: Building safely and affordably
description: Lesson 6
keywords: An AI model costs something for every question asked. On paid organisational Copilot plans, model-heavy features such as Chat, CLI, Spaces, the cloud agent, and similar agentic tools use AI credits — but code completions and next edit suggestions stay unlimited and are not billed in credits. Business includes 1,900 AI credits per user per month and Enterprise includes 3,900, with higher promotional allocations through 1 September 2026. Those credits are pooled across the whole billing entity, so heavy and light users balance out instead of every person being trapped inside a silo. Write down which part of your workflow needs unlimited autocomplete and which part truly needs model-heavy agentic work. That distinction is the basis of honest cost control.

title: Going beyond text
description: Lesson 7
keywords: AI isn't limited to text: some models can describe an image, transcribe an audio recording, or even generate an image from a description. For a course, this opens possibilities like marking a hand-drawn diagram or transcribing an oral presentation. These features need a bit more preparation, but the method stays the same: describe precisely what you want to Copilot, test, adjust. Try asking an AI model to describe or summarise one image or recording relevant to your own role.

title: Full example and conclusion
description: Lesson 8
keywords: To close this track, here is a complete example you can build end to end: an interactive quiz with automatic grading, scores saved to a database, and an AI explanation button for every missed question, all published online through GitHub. You now have every tool you need to build, test, publish, and evolve your own teaching apps. The only real limit now is the time you want to spend on it: thank you for following this track, and happy vibe coding! Write down one thing you'll build next with what you've learned in this course — then go build it.

title: Build a self-marking quiz in one sitting
description: You want a quiz your students can use to revise a chapter, without an external paid tool.
keywords: Open Copilot Chat and describe your quiz: “Build an HTML page with a 5-question multiple-choice quiz about [topic], showing a final score.” Read the generated code, test it in your browser, then ask one precise change at a time, e.g. “Add a short explanation under each question once it's answered.” Once you're happy with it, ask Copilot to add a “restart quiz” button. A working, customized quiz for your course, ready to publish. Ask Copilot to shuffle the question order on every launch.

title: Ground a diagram explainer with Copilot Spaces
description: You have slides, a scanned diagram, and tutor notes, and you want an accessible digital explainer instead of one more image embedded in a PDF.
keywords: Create a Space and upload the diagram image, the relevant slide text, and a plain-language caption. Ask Copilot Chat to turn that grounded material into an HTML/CSS explainer with labels, alt text, and a short glossary. Publish the approved version on GitHub Pages so students can revisit it outside class. A clearer, reusable explainer grounded in your own teaching material. Reuse the same Space for the next diagram-heavy topic instead of restating the context from scratch.

title: Generate exercise variants to reduce copying
description: You want several versions of the same exercise for different student groups.
keywords: Give Copilot Chat an existing exercise and ask: “Generate 4 variants of this exercise with different values but the same difficulty.” Ask for a shared marking scheme: “Add a marking scheme explaining each step.” Ask Copilot to export everything into one structured document. Several ready-to-distribute versions with a consistent marking scheme. Ask Copilot to also generate an accessible version for screen readers.

title: Automate a weighted grade calculator with agent mode
description: You manage a complex grading spreadsheet and want automatic weighted averages.
keywords: Describe your grading scheme to agent mode: “Build a page that calculates a weighted average from these categories: [list].” Review the plan the agent proposes before approving it. Ask it to add a CSV export to share results with colleagues. A reliable calculator matched to your own grading scheme. Connect it to a real database (see the Advanced track) to reuse it every semester.

title: Learn to code with Copilot as a tutor, not a crutch
description: You're new to programming and want to understand code, not just copy it.
keywords: Write a simple function yourself first, even an incomplete one. Ask Copilot Chat: “Explain line by line what this code does.” Then ask: “Quiz me on one thing to check I understood.” Real understanding of the code, not just copy-pasting. Ask Copilot for a slightly harder exercise on the same concept.

title: Build a shared revision site for your study group
description: Your study group wants one shared place to revise before the exam.
keywords: Describe the flashcard app you want to Copilot Chat. Use Copilot in the terminal to create the repository: describe what you want to do, Copilot suggests the exact git command. Share the GitHub Pages link with the group. A free, shared revision tool your whole group controls. Add a simple upvote system for the best flashcards.

title: Present your thesis or internship report online
description: You need to structure a long document and automate repetitive parts like a table of contents.
keywords: Ask Copilot to generate a site skeleton to present your thesis online (summary, chapters, appendices). Ask for an interactive table of contents built from your section headings. Add a contact page to receive feedback. An online, presentable version of your thesis, alongside the classic document. Ask Copilot to add keyword search across the content.

title: Build a portfolio grounded in your real project files
description: You want a portfolio site without rewriting every project description from scratch.
keywords: Create a Space with your README files, project screenshots, internship summary, and key links. Ask Copilot Chat to draft a one-page portfolio with project cards and short outcome-focused bullets. Refine the tone, then publish the result on GitHub Pages. A portfolio that is faster to build because the raw material is already grounded. Keep the Space updated each semester so future portfolio refreshes become a short editing pass.

title: Prototype an internal tool in one hour
description: A department asks for a small internal tool and you want a working prototype fast, before committing engineering time.
keywords: Describe the tool's core need to agent mode: “Build a page where staff can submit a request and see its status.” Review the proposed plan and let the agent build a first version. Ask for one realistic refinement, like form validation or a status colour code. A working prototype in under an hour, to validate the need before a full build. If it proves useful, plan a proper version with a real database and access control.

title: Document an existing script automatically
description: You've inherited an undocumented internal script and need to understand and document it fast.
keywords: Open the script and ask Copilot Chat: “Explain what this script does, step by step.” Ask: “Generate a README describing its purpose, inputs, and how to run it.” Ask Copilot to flag any risky or unclear parts of the code. Clear documentation for a script that previously only one person understood. Add the generated README directly to the script's repository.

title: Automate a deployment with GitHub Actions
description: You want a small site or tool to redeploy automatically whenever it changes.
keywords: Ask Copilot Chat: “Generate a GitHub Actions workflow that deploys this site to GitHub Pages on every push to main.” Add the suggested file to your repository and push a small change to test it. Ask Copilot to add a notification step if the deployment fails. A site that updates itself automatically, with no manual redeploy step. Reuse the same workflow file as a template for other internal projects.

title: Build an interactive onboarding checklist
description: New staff receive a long, static onboarding document that's easy to lose track of.
keywords: Describe the onboarding steps to Copilot Chat and ask for an interactive checklist page. Ask for progress to be saved so people can leave and come back. Ask Copilot to add a printable summary for HR records. A friendly, trackable onboarding experience for new colleagues. Personalize the checklist by role using a simple dropdown at the start.

title: Create a training feedback form in minutes
description: You need a quick way to collect feedback after a training session, without waiting on a survey tool licence.
keywords: Ask Copilot Chat to build a page with a 1-5 rating and a comments box. Ask it to store submissions so you can review them afterwards. Ask for a simple summary view showing the average rating. A working feedback form, live before the session even ends. Reuse the same page as a template for every future training session.

title: Build a leave-balance calculator
description: Staff keep asking HR how many vacation days they have left.
keywords: Describe your institution's leave policy to Copilot Chat. Ask it to build a small calculator that takes a start date and shows remaining days. Ask for a clear explanation shown alongside the result, in case of edge cases. A self-service tool that reduces repetitive questions to HR. Link it from the onboarding checklist above.

title: Run a live poll during a meeting
description: You want real-time feedback from staff during a town hall, without a paid polling tool.
keywords: Describe the question and options to Copilot Chat, following the same pattern as the Quick Poll example in the guided track. Test it yourself, then project the link during the meeting. Ask Copilot to add a live-updating results view. Instant, visible feedback from the room, without any external service. Reuse the exact same page for every future meeting, just changing the question.

title: Build a simple KPI dashboard
description: You want to track three or four numbers over time without a full BI tool.
keywords: Describe your KPIs to Copilot Chat and paste a few sample numbers. Ask it to build a clean, one-page dashboard summarizing them. Ask for a simple way to update the numbers each month. A lightweight dashboard you fully control and understand. Ask Copilot to add a small trend chart once you have a few months of data.

title: Turn strategy notes into a shareable one-pager with Copilot Spaces
description: You have meeting notes, KPI context, and a rough narrative, and you want a cleaner update than a wall of bullet points.
keywords: Create a Space with the strategy notes, the KPI sheet, and the core terms everyone uses internally. Ask Copilot Chat for a one-page summary with priorities, risks, and next actions in plain language. Review the wording, then publish or export the version you want to share. A clearer leadership one-pager grounded in your actual internal material. Reuse the same Space for monthly or quarterly updates so the vocabulary stays consistent.

title: Build a travel expense calculator
description: Staff often ask how much they'll be reimbursed for travel before submitting a claim.
keywords: Describe your reimbursement rules to Copilot Chat (distance, rate, caps). Ask it to build a small calculator based on those rules. Ask for a clear breakdown of the calculation shown to the user. A self-service estimator that reduces back-and-forth emails. Link it from the finance team's internal page.

title: Track a small recurring budget
description: You manage a small, recurring budget line and want a lighter alternative to a full spreadsheet.
keywords: Describe the budget categories to Copilot Chat. Ask for a simple page to log expenses with a running total. Ask for a monthly summary view. A lightweight tracker tailored to your exact categories. Export the data to a spreadsheet for the official records.

title: Turn pasted data into a sortable table
description: You regularly receive data as plain text or copy-pasted rows that are hard to work with.
keywords: Paste the raw data into Copilot Chat. Ask it to generate a clean, sortable HTML table from it. Ask for a search box to filter rows. A readable, searchable view of data that used to be a wall of text. Ask Copilot to add a CSV export button.

title: Clean a messy dataset with Copilot's help
description: You have a dataset full of inconsistencies (typos, missing values, mixed formats) before you can analyze it.
keywords: Describe the dataset's problems to Copilot Chat and paste a sample. Ask for a script that cleans and standardizes it. Review each cleaning rule before running it on the full dataset. A clean, analysis-ready dataset, with a documented script showing exactly what changed. Ask Copilot to add a summary report of what was cleaned and why.

title: Generate a first-pass statistical analysis script
description: You want a starting point for a standard analysis without writing boilerplate code from scratch.
keywords: Describe your data and research question to Copilot Chat. Ask for a script that runs the relevant statistical test and prints a clear summary. Ask Copilot to explain each step of the script in comments. A working analysis script you understand line by line, not a black box. Ask Copilot to add a simple chart of the results.

title: Build a research results page grounded in your figures
description: You want a public-facing explanation of your findings, but you also want the text to stay close to the abstract, figures, and talk notes you already trust.
keywords: Create a Space with the abstract, figure captions, poster text, and your plain-language summary notes. Ask Copilot Chat for a public results page with a short methods box and a clear summary for non-specialists. Review the text, then publish the page alongside the formal paper link. A research-results page that is grounded, accessible, and easier to reuse in talks or grant follow-up. Add a collaboration section and keep the Space as the source for future dissemination material.

title: Build an interactive resource catalogue
description: You want an easy way for students to browse recommended resources by topic.
keywords: Describe your resource list and categories to Copilot Chat. Ask for a searchable, filterable catalogue page. Ask for a simple way to add new resources over time. A living catalogue that's easier to browse than a static PDF list. Ask Copilot to add tags so resources can belong to several categories.

title: Generate an automatic FAQ page
description: You keep answering the same questions by email and want a public FAQ instead.
keywords: Paste your most common questions and answers into Copilot Chat. Ask for a clean FAQ page with a search box. Ask Copilot to group questions into clear categories. A self-service FAQ that reduces repetitive emails. Add a “still need help” contact link at the bottom.

title: Publish a campus events page from a grounded events pack
description: You have calendar exports, poster copy, and accessibility notes, and you want a cleaner events page that staff can update monthly.
keywords: Create a Space with the event titles, dates, descriptions, and accessibility notes. Ask Copilot Chat for a page that sorts events by date and highlights the next upcoming activities first. Publish the page on GitHub Pages and update the Space each month rather than rebuilding the page from scratch. A lightweight events page that is easier to maintain than a static poster archive. Add a “contact the organiser” block and reuse the same structure for every new month.

title: Turn one lab brief into three safe exercise variants
description: You have one practical brief and you want several variants that keep the same learning goals, rubric language, and safety wording.
keywords: Create a prompt file in the repository that asks for a variant, an answer key, and a short teacher note. Add custom instructions for tone, accessibility, and any lab-safety wording that must stay untouched. Ask Copilot Chat for three versions, then keep the approved set in the same course repository. A reusable variation workflow instead of rewriting the same exercise every semester. Keep the prompt file in the repo so colleagues can generate the next set from the same structure.

title: Let Copilot cloud agent refresh a course FAQ from issues
description: Students keep asking the same weekly questions and you want the FAQ page updated through reviewable pull requests rather than manual copy-paste.
keywords: Open an issue such as “Add this week’s recurring questions to the FAQ” and attach the grounded course Space if you already use one. Assign the issue to Copilot so the cloud agent drafts the page update on its own branch. Request Copilot code review on the pull request, review the wording yourself, then merge the approved update. A course FAQ that improves week by week without turning the teaching team into web maintainers. Use the same issue pattern after every lecture block so the FAQ becomes a living teaching asset.

title: Keep an internship or thesis project moving with Copilot Memory
description: You return to the same project every week and do not want to restate the context, stack, deadlines, and constraints from scratch every single time.
keywords: Store the stable project context in a Memory-enabled Copilot workflow and mirror the most important decisions in the repository README. Ask Copilot Chat for the next milestone, a progress summary, or a cleanup pass on the current code. Commit each approved change so the project history stays visible to supervisors and teammates. A steadier project rhythm with less time lost re-explaining the same background. Memory helps with continuity, but the real source of truth should still live in the repository.

title: Standardise helpdesk cleanup scripts with Agent skills
description: Different technicians solve the same account-cleanup or log-collection ticket in slightly different ways, and the variation creates avoidable risk.
keywords: Define an Agent skill with the approved script pattern, logging format, and rollback expectations. Ask Agent mode or Copilot CLI to adapt that skill to the current ticket instead of starting from a blank shell. Review the resulting script or diff before running it in the target environment. Repeatable internal automations with less copy-paste drift between technicians. Version the skill in GitHub so one update improves the whole team’s starting point.

title: Keep policy pages consistent with custom instructions
description: HR updates policies often, but headings, tone, required caveats, and inclusive wording drift from page to page.
keywords: Put the required tone, section order, inclusive wording, and approval notes in .github/copilot-instructions.md. Ask Copilot Chat to draft the updated page using those repository rules. Open a pull request and use Copilot code review as a second pair of eyes before publishing internally. Faster policy-page drafting with fewer formatting corrections later in the process. Extend the instructions file each time HR or Legal adds a new must-have section.

title: Create a custom agent that turns pilot ideas into comparable briefs
description: Several departments pitch small internal tools at once, and leadership needs a comparable brief for each proposal before deciding what to fund.
keywords: Define a custom agent that must always output the same sections: problem, users, low-risk first version, data sensitivity, and next step. Run that agent in separate GitHub Copilot app sessions, one proposal per worktree. Compare the resulting briefs and PR summaries side by side instead of comparing informal hallway requests. A reviewable pipeline of lightweight prototypes instead of a backlog of vague requests. Keep the winning briefs in a shared gallery repository so the next team can fork an existing idea instead of starting from zero.

title: Generate monthly budget notes in one shared house style
description: Finance turns the same export into monthly comments, but wording and tables vary from person to person.
keywords: Store formatting rules and mandatory headings in custom instructions. Create a prompt file that asks for a variance summary, top exceptions, and next actions from the pasted export. Run the prompt each month, then review the draft note in a pull request before it circulates. More consistent monthly reporting with visible rules in the repository. This is especially useful when several people rotate across the same reporting workflow.

title: Ask a lab scheduling system for utilisation patterns through MCP
description: A research platform team wants to understand which equipment slots stay underused without manually exporting and reshaping the same files every month.
keywords: Connect Copilot to the approved scheduling system through an MCP server or another governed connector. Ask for utilisation by day, room, or lab in plain language to identify obvious underuse patterns. Let Agent mode generate the dashboard or notebook that reproduces the answer so the method stays inspectable. A faster path from operational question to reproducible utilisation view. Keep the connection scoped to approved data only and reuse the same prompts each semester.

title: Build a citation-help assistant for the library
description: Library staff keep answering the same “How do I cite this?” questions across guides, workshops, and helpdesk messages.
keywords: Create a Copilot Space with citation guides, local library policy notes, and worked examples. Ask Copilot Chat to draft a searchable help page or chatbot copy grounded in that material. Publish the approved version on GitHub Pages and keep the Space fresh when the guide changes. A grounded citation helper that points people back to the library’s own guidance. Refresh the Space whenever the library updates its style-guide pages or exceptions.

title: Ship a small incident-reporting form for campus facilities
description: Facilities staff need a lightweight way to collect location, photo, urgency, and follow-up status for minor incidents without waiting for a full platform replacement.
keywords: Ask Agent mode to scaffold the form, confirmation screen, and the simplest useful storage pattern for a pilot. Use Copilot code review to check field labels, validation, and the clarity of the follow-up flow. Pilot the first version in one building before deciding whether it deserves a bigger system. A practical reporting flow that can start small and still stay reviewable. If the pilot works, move it into a shared repo with a code owner instead of leaving it on one laptop.
